claims.text: Subgrain-boundary density and stability primarily govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys.
Fine, stable subgrain boundaries act as barriers and channels for dislocation motion.
A dense population of fine, stable subgrain boundaries promotes more spatially uniform plastic deformation.
Plastic deformation accommodated by fine, stable subgrain boundaries delays crack initiation and propagation.
Coalescence or coarsening of subgrain boundaries at elevated temperature reduces their ability to accommodate dislocations.
Coarse or unstable subgrain boundaries cause strain localization and premature fracture.
Thermomechanical treatments can systematically vary subgrain-boundary density without changing alloy chemistry.
Increasing the density of fine, stable subgrain boundaries will increase high-temperature strain to failure relative to the as-processed baseline.
Increasing the density of fine, stable subgrain boundaries will improve toughness and delay crack propagation relative to the as-processed baseline.
Subgrain-boundary coarsening will diminish high-temperature plasticity and fracture resistance.
The proposed mechanism should remain operative under elevated temperature and high neutron or thermal flux.
The proposed comparison is applicable only when alloy chemistry is constant and major phase transformations and precipitate variations are absent.
Precipitate distribution may affect the quantitative influence of subgrain boundaries on deformation.
Prior studies link grain or twin-boundary microstructures to dislocation behavior, deformation distribution, ductility, and toughness-related plasticity.
High-temperature deformation mechanisms in a Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti refractory high-entropy alloy change with temperature, including twinning, grain-boundary cavitation, and dynamic recrystallization.
